questions.prompt: Which file is traditionally used to define TestNG suites, groups and parallel settings?
questions.explanation: testng.xml describes suites and tests; Maven Surefire can point at it with suiteXmlFiles.
enabled = false excludes the method from the run.

questions.prompt: Which attribute makes a test run only after another test method has passed?
questions.explanation: dependsOnMethods declares a hard dependency: if the dependency fails, the dependent test is skipped. priority only influences order.

questions.prompt: In what order do these tests run (single thread, default settings)?
questions.explanation: Lower priority runs first, and the default priority is 0. So c (priority -1) runs first, then a (0), then b (1).

questions.prompt: This SoftAssert test passes even when both checks fail. Why?
options: assertAll() is never called, so collected failures are never reported
questions.explanation: SoftAssert gathers failures and throws only when assertAll() runs, typically at the end of the test.

questions.prompt: Which statements about TestNG groups are true? Select all that apply.
options: A test can belong to several groups
testng.xml can include or exclude groups
Groups replace the need for assertions
questions.explanation: Groups are labels for selection and group-level setup; they do not verify anything.

options: Runs the test once with five retries
Runs the method five times, concurrently on up to five threads
Fails if the test takes more than five seconds
questions.explanation: invocationCount repeats a method; threadPoolSize runs those invocations in parallel. It is a quick way to stress a piece of code or check thread safety.

questions.prompt: Your suite uses `dependsOnMethods` to chain 30 tests (create user, then log in, then order, ...). One early failure skips 29 tests and nobody knows their real status. What should you change?
options: Make each test set up its own preconditions (via API calls or fixtures) so tests are independent; keep dependencies only for genuine prerequisites
Put all steps in one huge test
questions.explanation: Long dependency chains hide information and make the suite fragile. Independent tests with fast setup give each behaviour its own pass/fail signal. One huge test has the same problem in a different shape.

questions.prompt: You add an IRetryAnalyzer that retries every failed test 3 times. Flaky failures disappear from reports. What is the risk and how should you mitigate it?
options: Real intermittent bugs and flaky tests get hidden; report retried-then-passed tests separately, limit retries to known-flaky categories, and track them for fixing
TestNG ignores retry analyzers in CI
questions.explanation: Retries trade signal for green builds. Visibility (marking them flaky) and a plan to fix them keep the safety net from becoming a blindfold.

coding.title: Predict TestNG run order
coding.prompt:
Write `runOrder(tests)` where each test is `{ name, priority = 0, dependsOn = [] }`. Return the method names in run order using these simplified TestNG rules:

1. A test only runs after all the tests it depends on.
2. Among tests that are ready, pick the lowest priority, then alphabetical name.

Throw an `Error('cycle')` if dependencies make it impossible.

```js
runOrder([{ name: 'b', priority: 1 }, { name: 'a' }, { name: 'c', priority: -1 }])
// ['c', 'a', 'b']
```
coding.explanation: Repeatedly choosing the best ready test is a topological sort with a tie-breaker. Dependencies override priority: a priority -5 test still waits for its dependency. If no test is ready but some remain, the dependencies form a cycle, which TestNG also rejects.
hints: Keep a Set of finished tests.
Each round, filter tests whose dependsOn are all done, then sort by priority then name.
If nothing is ready but tests remain, throw Error('cycle').

tests.name: cycle detected
tests.code: let m=''; try { runOrder([{name:'x', dependsOn:['y']},{name:'y', dependsOn:['x']}]); } catch(e) { m = e.message; } assertEqual(m, 'cycle')

coding.title: Which tests get skipped?
coding.explanation: Each test's result depends on its dependencies' results, so a memoised recursive resolve computes them in the right order. A skip propagates through the chain just like in TestNG, which is why one early failure can hide the status of many later tests.
hints: Resolve each test recursively from its dependencies.
If any dependency is not 'pass', the test is 'skip' regardless of the failed list.
Memoise results in an object so each test is resolved once.
